column4: 79% of nonprofits now run five or more systems beyond their main CRM — up from 62% just one year ago.↵↵That jump is not a coincidence. It reflects a category of organizations that kept adding tools to solve specific problems without accounting for the cost of connecting them.↵↵Each integration point runs $1,200–$6,000/year in middleware costs. Four connections can put a mid-sized nonprofit at $5,000–$24,000/year before a single staff hour is counted.↵↵Staff at multi-system organizations spend 20–30% of their total work time on cross-system data entry — about one full-time equivalent position on a team of five.↵↵The data quality problem compounds the cost. 54% of nonprofits identify incomplete or inaccurate data as a major obstacle. Every manual transfer between systems is an opportunity for error.↵↵Fragmentation looks like efficiency until you price it honestly.↵↵GrantPipe runs donor management and grant compliance in one system — no middleware, no reconciliation tax. If the math has started to look wrong on your current stack, it may be time to run the numbers.

VAWA confidentiality is not a best practice. It is a federal prohibition.↵↵Section 13925(b)(2) of the Violence Against Women Act bars any VAWA grantee from disclosing personally identifying information about a service recipient — to funders, federal systems, or any third party — without informed, written, reasonably time-limited consent.↵↵PII under VAWA includes names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and any information that could be used to identify or locate an individual.↵↵Most commercial CRMs are not configured to honor this rule by default. If a funder, federal program officer, or support staffer can access your client records through shared logins or integrations, that system may already be out of compliance.↵↵Intentional violations carry consequences: funding termination, OIG referral, and civil liability.↵↵The VAWA 2022 reauthorization (Pub. L. 117-103, Division W) strengthened these protections and extended them explicitly to tribal organizations and LGBTQ+ survivors.↵↵The PMT portal receives aggregate service counts — never individual client records. That distinction is not a technicality. It is the architecture.

Most organizations updated their journal entry practices after FASB ASU 2020-07. Far fewer updated their footnote disclosures.↵↵ASU 2020-07 — effective for fiscal years beginning after June 15, 2021 — requires nonprofits to present contributed nonfinancial assets as a separate line and disclose by category: the valuation technique, fair value hierarchy level, whether assets were monetized or used directly, and any donor restrictions.↵↵The footnote is not the same as the general contributions policy note that existed before.↵↵Common gaps after adoption: organizations list food donations as 'valued at fair value' without stating they used USDA wholesale prices as the basis. Or they disclose that legal services were received without identifying that the value used was the attorney's standard billing rate.↵↵Under 2 CFR 200.306, in-kind contributions used as federal grant match must be valued using comparable market prices with documentation that is verifiable by auditors.↵↵Stale valuations from the year a recurring in-kind relationship began — the law firm that has donated services for three years, still valued at 2022 billing rates — are a quiet audit risk.↵↵If the footnote has not been reviewed since adoption year, that is the place to start.

'Award period' and 'period of performance' mean the same thing. What they authorize is narrower than most people assume.↵↵Under 2 CFR 200.77, the period of performance is the time during which a non-federal entity may incur new obligations against the award. Costs incurred before the start date or after the end date are unallowable — regardless of when the invoice is paid.↵↵Some federal awards include a liquidation period (commonly 90 days after the end date) during which costs incurred before the end date may still be paid. That is not the same as an extension of the project period.↵↵A supply invoice received 10 days after the end date for goods delivered during the grant period may be allowable during the liquidation window. A purchase order issued after the end date is not, regardless of when payment clears.↵↵The start date is also often misread. Some awards specify a project start date weeks before the award letter arrives. Costs incurred from the project start date — not the date the letter was received — are allowable.↵↵Enter the exact dates from the Notice of Award. Not from the application. Not from an email confirmation. From the Notice of Award.

Keela's grant module does what it says: tracks a grant name, amount, deadline, and status. That covers the first list of requirements.↵↵Government and foundation funders typically require the second list: budget tracking by line item with expenditure monitoring, restricted fund separation with flagging of misallocations, compliance milestone checklists tied to award terms, and funder report templates that pull from actual expenditure data.↵↵The gap between those two lists creates operational problems the moment a program officer asks for a budget-to-actual report.↵↵A system that tracks deadlines without enforcing fund separation does not reduce compliance risk. It creates the appearance of oversight without the substance.↵↵According to Omatic's 2025 report, nearly half of nonprofits are considering switching CRMs in the next 12 months — driven by feature gaps and growth, not cost. The trigger is usually not general dissatisfaction. It is one repeated workflow that breaks: the moment when staff cannot get from transaction to funder report without building the context manually in another tool.↵↵Before evaluating alternatives, document the three reports that currently cause the most delay. A credible replacement should handle those natively.

The grants manager departure takes 3–5 years of institutional knowledge out the door in two weeks.↵↵The factual knowledge — which grants are active, where the files are, what the deadlines are — is the easiest to recover if the system has it. The tactical and relational knowledge is harder.↵↵Tactical knowledge sounds like 'we've always done it this way': the federal budget modification threshold is 10% but the program officer won't flag changes under 12%. The foundation's report deadline is October 15, not end of October. This knowledge exists but has never been written down.↵↵Relational knowledge — funder preferences, relationship history, what the program officer emphasized in the last renewal conversation — mostly leaves with the person.↵↵The transition protocol that limits the damage: one structured session per active grant with the outgoing manager (60–90 minutes; do not combine all grants), a grant file audit before the last day, transfer of every portal credential through a secure credential store, and a named interim owner for every compliance task due in the 60 days following departure.↵↵The overlap period needed for a portfolio of 5–10 active grants is two to four weeks minimum.↵↵Less than two weeks is not enough for adequate knowledge transfer.

A funder report that only documents compliance misses the relationship opportunity.↵↵A well-structured report does four things: demonstrates that the work is happening, shows the organization is honest about challenges, shows the money is being managed carefully, and connects the funder's investment to the effects they care about.↵↵The section most reports omit is the one that matters most for the relationship: a direct request for funder engagement. A site visit. A conversation about renewal timing. A specific question about funder priorities for next year.↵↵For foundation reports, the budget-vs-actual comparison should flag any cumulative variance above 10% with an explanation. A report that shows 70% of the budget period elapsed and 45% of funds expended without an explanation is not reassuring — it raises questions the report should have answered.↵↵For federal reports, the SF-425 is not the narrative report. Both need to be filed, on different schedules, through different systems.↵↵GrantPipe's free Funder Report Template covers both formats — private foundation and federal agency — with the financial summary tables, budget variance section, and the submission checklist that confirms everything was filed and saved before you call the report done.↵↵Download it at grantpipe.com.

Virtuous is a donor engagement platform. GrantPipe is a grant compliance platform. They are not competing for the same operating problem.↵↵Virtuous wins when the organization's primary challenge is major donor cultivation — sophisticated automated journeys, prospect enrichment, and a daily workflow designed around the development director's relationship management tasks.↵↵Grant compliance in Virtuous is not a core feature. Organizations managing multiple awards with recurring reporting obligations still need a parallel system.↵↵The test is straightforward: count how many hours per month your team spends on tasks that would not exist if grant compliance and donor records shared a system. If the answer is more than 10 hours, that coordination overhead likely exceeds any premium Virtuous charges for its fundraising automation.↵↵On pricing: Virtuous operates on a quote basis. Community estimates for mid-sized organizations run $400–$1,000+/month. GrantPipe publishes flat tiers starting at $329/month.↵↵Grant funding represents more than 40% of revenue for the average mid-sized nonprofit in the $500K–$5M range (Nonprofit Finance Fund 2024). At that revenue composition, a donor-first platform that does not carry the compliance layer will always require a second system. The cost of that second system — in staff time and reporting risk — is the real comparison.

Six fund accounting platforms, one distinction that matters before evaluating any of them.↵↵Sage Intacct ($10,000–$30,000+/yr): The strongest option for organizations above $5M that need FASB ASC 958 compliance built into the data model and AICPA-recognized reporting. Implementation runs $15,000–$50,000 additional through a certified partner.↵↵MIP Fund Accounting ($5,000–$20,000+/yr): Purpose-built for nonprofits, strong federal compliance and SEFA capability, integrated payroll for personnel cost allocation. Interface is dated but the fund accounting depth is genuine. Best fit $2M–$10M.↵↵NetSuite ($20,000–$60,000+/yr): Full ERP for multi-entity structures. Cost-complexity ratio is unfavorable for most mid-sized nonprofits.↵↵QuickBooks Online ($360–$2,400/yr): Class tracking is not fund accounting. It approximates it. Auditors increasingly flag it for organizations above $1M in grant revenue.↵↵Xero ($180–$936/yr): Same limitation as QuickBooks for fund accounting purposes. Adequate for small nonprofits where the board accepts non-fund-accounting software.↵↵Aplos ($708–$2,388/yr): True fund accounting at an accessible price. Federal compliance capabilities are basic — not appropriate for heavy federal award portfolios.↵↵The distinction that matters: fund accounting handles the financial record. Grant management handles the operational record — award terms, reporting deadlines, funder relationships. Most organizations need both. They are usually different systems.

The setup work done in week one determines how easy or difficult compliance management will be for the entire grant period.↵↵Entering only a grant name and a total award amount is not a setup. It is a placeholder.↵↵A complete setup requires seven fields entered before any spending begins.↵↵The project period — exact start and end dates from the Notice of Award, not from the application or from an email — because costs outside these dates are unallowable under 2 CFR 200.77.↵↵The award amount by approved budget category: personnel, fringe, supplies, travel, equipment, indirect, and any program-specific lines. Without line-item budgets, the system cannot flag when a category is approaching its limit.↵↵The restriction type: program-restricted, time-restricted, geography-restricted, or unrestricted.↵↵The complete reporting schedule — every deadline for the full period of performance, not just the final report.↵↵The funder contact record — program officer name, title, email, phone — linked to the grant, not sitting in someone's inbox.↵↵Prior approval requirements from the award terms, documented before program leads start making operational decisions.↵↵The accounting system grant code, confirmed with finance on the same day, so expenditures code correctly from day one.↵↵GrantPipe's setup workflow walks through each field in order, with the reporting calendar built automatically from the project period and reporting schedule. The hour invested in a complete setup pays for itself dozens of times over the grant period.
